title: Boss: the order service on the release branch
summary: The integration suite is red on the release branch: fix the endpoint from the failing test's stack trace, pin the JSON contract the mobile app depends on, and prove the database constraints with SQLite.

steps.title: Release 4.2 is blocked
body: System.Collections.Generic.KeyNotFoundException : The given key 'cup' was not present in the dictionary.
at OrdersApi.<>c.<Create>b__0_0(OrderIn input, Catalog catalog, OrderBook book) in OrdersApi.cs:line 13

Two things to read here. TestServer passes an unhandled exception straight to the test, so the stack trace points at the handler line (in production the same request is a bare 500). And the second failure is not an exception at all: the endpoint happily created an order with quantity 0.
The API contract says: unknown products are **422** with a problem-details body, and a quantity below 1 is **400**.

steps.title: Fix the endpoint
prompt: Fix `OrdersApi` so the integration checks (`OrdersApiChecks`, run over a TestServer when you press **Run checks**) pass:
- `POST /orders` with `{ "sku": "mug", "quantity": 2 }` returns **201**, `Location: /orders/{id}` and the order (`totalCents` is price times quantity);
- an unknown SKU returns **422** with a problem-details body (`Results.Problem(statusCode: 422, title: "Unknown product")`);
starter: public record OrderIn(string Sku, int Quantity);
public record OrderOut(int Id, string Sku, int Quantity, long TotalCents);
public sealed class Catalog { public Dictionary<string, long> PricesCents { get; } = new() { ["mug"] = 800, ["tea"] = 450 }; }
public sealed class OrderBook { public List<OrderOut> Orders { get; } = []; }
app.MapPost("/orders", (OrderIn input, Catalog catalog, OrderBook book) =>
var order = new OrderOut(book.Orders.Count + 1, input.Sku, input.Quantity, price * input.Quantity);
book.Orders.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Id == id) is { } o ? Results.Ok(o) : Results.NotFound());
solution: public record OrderIn(string Sku, int Quantity);
public record OrderOut(int Id, string Sku, int Quantity, long TotalCents);
public sealed class Catalog { public Dictionary<string, long> PricesCents { get; } = new() { ["mug"] = 800, ["tea"] = 450 }; }
public sealed class OrderBook { public List<OrderOut> Orders { get; } = []; }
app.MapPost("/orders", (OrderIn input, Catalog catalog, OrderBook book) =>
return Results.ValidationProblem(new Dictionary<string, string[]> { ["quantity"] = ["Order at least one."] });
return Results.Problem(statusCode: 422, title: "Unknown product", detail: $"There is no product '{input.Sku}'.");
var order = new OrderOut(book.Orders.Count + 1, input.Sku, input.Quantity, price * input.Quantity);
book.Orders.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Id == id) is { } o ? Results.Ok(o) : Results.NotFound());
template: static async Task<(WebApplication App, HttpClient Client)> StartAsync()
var response = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/orders", new { sku = "mug", quantity = 2 }, Ct);
var response = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/orders", new { sku = "cup", quantity = 1 }, Ct);
var response = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/orders", new { sku = "mug", quantity }, Ct);
await client.PostAsJsonAsync("/orders", new { sku = "tea", quantity = 3 }, Ct);
hints: Read the stack trace's handler line: the indexer `catalog.PricesCents[input.Sku]` throws for an unknown key.
`TryGetValue` lets you return `Results.Problem(statusCode: 422, title: "Unknown product")` instead.
Check the quantity first: `if (input.Quantity < 1) return Results.ValidationProblem(new Dictionary<string, string[]> { ["quantity"] = ["Order at least one."] });`.
steps.explain: Validate input, then look things up with `TryGetValue`, and turn each failure into the status code the contract promises. The integration checks prove it through the real pipeline, problem-details content type included.

steps.title: Pin the JSON contract
prompt: The mobile app parses `GET /orders/{id}` and crashes on any change to its shape. The read API, compiled beside your tests:
public record OrderView(int Id, string Sku, long TotalCents, OrderStatus Status, DateOnly PlacedOn);
The agreed contract for order 42 is exactly:

Write `public class OrderContractTests` with at least **2** tests over a TestServer: the exact JSON body of order 42, and 404 for another id. Five planted bugs, each a "harmless" change someone might make to the C# types.
solution: static async Task<(WebApplication App, HttpClient Client)> StartAsync()

target: public record OrderView(int Id, string Sku, long TotalCents, OrderStatus Status, DateOnly PlacedOn);

mutants.name: the status is sent as a number
an internal field leaks into the response
the date became a date and time

hints: Reuse the TestServer helper from the lesson, with `OrderReadApi.Create(builder)`.
`client.GetStringAsync("/orders/42", Ct)` gives the raw body; compare it with the contract as a raw string literal: `"""{"id":42,...}"""`.
Deserializing into `OrderView` would hide most of these bugs: the C# side changes with them. A contract test looks at the JSON itself.
steps.explain: Each planted change compiles, passes every C# test that uses the same types, and breaks the mobile app. Only a test on the bytes on the wire sees it. Verify snapshots are the same idea, with a diff tool and an approved file.

steps.title: Prove the database constraints
prompt: The CRM model, compiled beside your tests (EF Core with SQLite is available):
public class Customer { public int Id { get; set; } public string Email { get; set; } = ""; public List<Address> Addresses { get; set; } = []; }
public class Address { public int Id { get; set; } public string City { get; set; } = ""; public int CustomerId { get; set; } }

Write `public sealed class CrmDbTests : IDisposable` on SQLite in memory with at least **2** tests: saving a second customer with the same e-mail throws `DbUpdateException`; deleting a customer deletes their addresses. Two planted bugs.
solution: db.Customers.Add(new Customer { Email = "ada@example.com", Addresses = [new Address { City = "London" }, new Address { City = "Leeds" }] });

target: public class Customer { public int Id { get; set; } public string Email { get; set; } = ""; public List<Address> Addresses { get; set; } = []; }
public class Address { public int Id { get; set; } public string City { get; set; } = ""; public int CustomerId { get; set; } }

mutants.name: the unique index on Email is gone
deleting a customer no longer cascades

hints: Open the connection in the constructor and call `EnsureCreated()` once; create a new `CrmDb` per unit of work so each step really goes to the database.
The unique test: add, save, add the same e-mail again, and `Assert.Throws<DbUpdateException>(() => db.SaveChanges())`.
The cascade test: save a customer with two addresses, remove the customer in a fresh context, then count addresses in a third context.
steps.explain: Constraints are behaviour too, and they live in the database, so only a real engine can test them. Using a fresh context for each step stops EF's change tracker from answering in place of the database.
